learningObjectives.title: Coordination and control – the nervous system
Coordination and control – the endocrine system

questions.q: What two structures make up the central nervous system (CNS)?
options: The brain and the spinal cord
The brain and the sensory neurones
The spinal cord and the receptors
The nerves and the effectors
questions.explain: The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord, which coordinate the body's responses.

questions.q: Which type of neurone carries electrical impulses from a receptor to the central nervous system?
options: Sensory neurone
Motor neurone
Relay neurone
Effector neurone
questions.explain: Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the pathway of a reflex arc?
options: Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector → response
Stimulus → effector → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → receptor → response
Receptor → stimulus → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → effector → response
Stimulus → receptor → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → effector → response
questions.explain: In a reflex arc the impulse passes from receptor via sensory, relay and motor neurones to the effector.

questions.q: What is the name of the junction between two neurones?
options: A synapse
A dendrite
An axon
A receptor
questions.explain: A synapse is the small gap between two neurones where signals are passed on.

questions.q: How is a nerve impulse transmitted across a synapse?
options: A chemical neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap
An electrical current jumps directly across the gap
The two neurones fuse together to pass the impulse
Blood carries the impulse between the neurones
questions.explain: At a synapse a chemical neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap and triggers an impulse in the next neurone.

questions.q: Which region of the brain is mainly responsible for coordinating balance and muscular movement?
options: The cerebellum
The cerebrum
The medulla
The hypothalamus
questions.explain: The cerebellum coordinates balance, posture and fine muscular movement.

questions.q: A person steps on a sharp pin and immediately lifts their foot away. What is the effector in this reflex?
options: A muscle in the leg
The sharp pin
The sensory neurone
The spinal cord
questions.explain: The effector is the muscle that contracts to move the foot away from the stimulus.

questions.q: Which hormone reduces the concentration of glucose in the blood?
options: Insulin
Glucagon
Adrenaline
Thyroxine
questions.explain: Insulin lowers blood glucose by causing cells to take up glucose and the liver to store it as glycogen.

questions.q: Which organ produces the hormone insulin?
options: The pancreas
The liver
The thyroid gland
The adrenal gland
questions.explain: The pancreas produces insulin, which regulates blood glucose concentration.

questions.q: What effect does glucagon have when blood glucose concentration falls too low?
options: It makes the liver convert glycogen into glucose, raising blood glucose
It makes the liver convert glucose into glycogen, lowering blood glucose
It causes cells to take in more glucose from the blood
It stops the pancreas detecting blood glucose levels
questions.explain: Glucagon stimulates the liver to break down glycogen into glucose, raising blood glucose levels.

questions.q: A student about to sit a difficult exam feels their heart racing. Which gland has released the hormone responsible for this response?
options: The adrenal glands
The pancreas
The thyroid gland
The ovaries
questions.explain: The adrenal glands release adrenaline, which increases heart rate as part of the 'fight or flight' response.

questions.q: What is the underlying cause of Type 1 diabetes?
options: The pancreas does not produce enough insulin
Body cells stop responding to insulin
The liver produces too much glucagon
The kidneys remove too much glucose from the blood
questions.explain: In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas fails to produce enough insulin, so it must be given by injection.

questions.q: Which hormone triggers ovulation (the release of an egg) during the menstrual cycle?
options: Luteinising hormone (LH)
Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)
Progesterone
Oestrogen
questions.explain: A surge in LH from the pituitary gland triggers ovulation at around day 14.

questions.q: What is the role of follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) in the menstrual cycle?
options: It causes an egg to mature and stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen
It triggers the release of an egg from the ovary
It maintains the lining of the uterus during pregnancy
It causes the uterus lining to break down
questions.explain: FSH, released by the pituitary gland, causes an egg to mature and stimulates oestrogen production.

questions.q: During the first half of the menstrual cycle the lining of the uterus thickens ready for a fertilised egg. Which hormone is mainly responsible for this thickening?
options: Oestrogen
Luteinising hormone (LH)
Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)
Insulin
questions.explain: Oestrogen, produced by the ovaries, causes the uterus lining to thicken and repair.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares nervous and hormonal (endocrine) responses?
options: Nervous responses are fast and short-lived; hormonal responses are slower and longer-lasting
Nervous responses are slow and long-lasting; hormonal responses are fast and short-lived
Both nervous and hormonal responses are equally fast and short-lived
Hormonal responses use electrical impulses while nervous responses use chemicals in the blood
questions.explain: The nervous system gives fast, brief responses via electrical impulses, while hormones give slower, longer-lasting responses via the blood.

questions.q: What does the term 'homeostasis' mean?
options: Maintaining a constant internal environment in the body
Increasing the rate of chemical reactions in cells
Removing all waste products from the blood
Producing hormones from endocrine glands
questions.explain: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes.

questions.q: When the body becomes too hot, how does vasodilation help to cool it down?
options: Blood vessels near the skin surface widen, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost
Blood vessels near the skin surface narrow, so less heat is lost from the blood
Muscles contract rapidly to release heat energy
Sweat glands stop producing sweat to conserve water
questions.explain: Vasodilation widens skin blood vessels so more blood flows near the surface, increasing heat loss.

questions.q: How does shivering help to raise body temperature when a person is too cold?
options: Muscles contract rapidly and respiration releases heat energy
Blood vessels near the skin widen to bring in warm blood
Sweat glands release sweat that warms the skin as it evaporates
The hairs on the skin lie flat to trap warm air
questions.explain: Shivering makes muscles contract rapidly, and the extra respiration this requires releases heat.

questions.q: Shortly after eating a meal rich in carbohydrate, a healthy person's blood glucose rises. How does the body respond to return it to normal?
options: The pancreas releases insulin, causing the liver to store glucose as glycogen
The pancreas releases glucagon, causing the liver to release more glucose
The adrenal glands release adrenaline to raise blood glucose further
The kidneys stop removing glucose so the level stays high
questions.explain: Rising blood glucose triggers insulin release, causing the liver and cells to take up glucose and store it as glycogen.
